Learning Objectives
Understand the difference between primary and secondary bone healing.
Understand how the forces applied to a fracture site affect healing.
Describe the functions of plates and how plates can be used to allow for primary or secondary
bone healing.
Describe the difference in healing between plates and nails and how to increase stability with
the use of nails
Describe how to increase stability by modifying external fixation constructs, and explain the
difference between temporary and definitive external fixation.

Bone Mechanics: Stress-Strain Curve and Fracture Mechanics
The mechanical behavior of bone and other biomaterials can be depicted by a stress-strain
curve.
The degree of strain and motion observed at a fracture site determines the type of fracture
healing that occurs.

Bone Mechanics: Stress-Strain Curve and Fracture Mechanics
Stress refers to the load applied to bone (or force) divided by the cross-sectional area of
the bone. Strain refers to the resultant deformation of bone (or change in length) relative
to the original length of the bone. Load and deformation (or stress and strain) are
linearly proportional until the yield point is reached. The slope of the linear portion of
the stress-strain curve is defined as the stiffness or rigidity (the load required to deform
bone a given amount). This linear region of the stress-strain curve is referred to as the
elastic zone because a material will return to its original shape after the deforming force
is removed. Beyond the yield point, the slope of the stress-strain curve decreases,
indicating that less force is required to create additional deformation. As additional load
is applied to bone, the ultimate load is eventually reached, resulting in fracture.
Intact bone can tolerate strains as great as 2% before fracture. Primary (direct) bone
healing requires strain at the fracture site to be less than 2% (achieved via rigid fixation
methods). To stimulate secondary fracture repair, a degree of motion is necessary, but
excess strain will inhibit healing. Strain of 2% to 10% induces secondary bone healing.
The degree of motion at the fracture site must result in a strain on the healing unit lower
than its breaking strain for that material to bridge the fracture gap. Through the staged
process of secondary bone healing, the initial soft callus becomes stiffer and reduces
interfragmentary movement to allow for the formation of hard callus. As a result, the
strain experienced at the fracture gap progressively decreases1,2 (Resource 1).
Bone Healing: Primary (Direct) Versus Secondary

Bone healing occurs via primary (direct) or secondary repair depending on the reduction,
normal stresses at the fracture site, and method of fixation.
Primary (direct) bone repair requires anatomic reduction, compression with no fracture gap,
and rigid fixation.
Secondary bone healing occurs in five stages: hematoma, inflammation, soft callus, hard
callus, and remodeling.

Bone Healing: Primary (Direct) Versus Secondary
Primary (direct) bone healing follows anatomic fracture reduction, bony compression
without gap, and rigid surgical fixation. The strain of the fracture must be less than 2% to
allow for primary bone repair, necessitating rigid fixation with no interfragmentary
motion at the fracture site (absolute stability). In addition, no gap (<0.1 mm) can exist
between the fractured bone surfaces, which requires anatomic reduction with
compression. Unlike secondary bone healing, no inflammatory phase occurs during
primary bone repair. The process of primary bone repair involves multiple cutting cones
that cross the fracture site. Cutting cones consist of a leading collection of osteoclasts,
often described as a spearhead, which create cavities in the bone. These cavities are
filled by a central blood vessel, and the surrounding walls are lined by osteoblasts, which
form new bone.
In fractures that have been fixed rigidly but contain a residual gap, gap healing may
occur. Cutting cones are unable to cross residual gaps. Therefore, immature lamellar
bone is initially deposited at the fracture site to close the residual gap. Cutting cones can
then traverse the fracture site. Although primary bone healing does not require the
multiple steps involved in secondary bone repair, it is a much slower process.
In contrast to primary bone healing (which requires absolute stability), secondary bone
healing occurs in an environment that allows for controlled interfragmentary motion at
the fracture site (relative stability). Casts, braces, external fixators, intramedullary nails,
and plates can create an environment of relative stability.

Secondary bone healing occurs through five stages that progressively increase fracture
stiffness. The first stage involves hematoma formation as a result of bleeding from
fractured bone surfaces and the surrounding soft tissue. A fibrin clot is formed that is
rich in signaling factors that recruit inflammatory cells and blood vessels to the fracture
site. Fracture hematoma provides little stability but tolerates strains as great as 100%.
Next, the inflammatory phase brings neutrophils to the hematoma, which are
subsequently replaced by infiltrating macrophages. This mononuclear cell line engulfs
fibrin and entrapped red blood cells. Inflammatory cytokines (including tumor necrosis
factor α, interleukin [IL]-1, IL-6, IL-11, and IL-18) play an important role in recruiting
inflammatory cells, stimulating angiogenesis at the fracture site, and guiding the
differentiation of osteoclasts and osteoblasts.
In the third phase of this process, fibroblasts and chondrocytes deposit a
fibrocartilaginous matrix to form a soft callus bridging the fracture ends. The external
aspect of the soft callus is created by surrounding muscle and periosteum, whereas
medullary tissue and bone cortex contribute to the internal callus. Soft-callus formation
increases fracture stability but allows for strain as great as 20%. Initially, this tissue strain
is too high to allow for cartilage or bone formation; however, as the soft callus grows in
volume, fracture stability increases, and tissue strain eventually reaches a point at which
bone formation can occur via endochondral ossification.
During endochondral ossification, mesenchymal stem cells are recruited and
differentiate into chondroblasts and osteoblasts, which ultimately ossify the surrounding
matrix, the fourth phase of secondary fracture healing. As the callus stiffness increases,
regions in the callus fall below the normal strain of bone (2%). Hard callus formation can
then occur via endochondral ossification and calcification of the soft callus. Hard callus
continues to be deposited in the form of woven bone.
In the final phase of secondary bone healing, woven bone is replaced by mechanically
stronger lamellar bone via remodeling. Remodeling occurs in response to the
mechanical requirements of bone as the mature bone is able to bear increasing loads3
(Resource 2).

Biomechanical Principles
Spectrum of Stability
Fixation construct stability occurs on a spectrum, with flexible constructs promoting relative
stability and secondary bone healing with callus formation and rigid constructs promoting
absolute stability and primary bone healing.
Rigid constructs with high stiffness are load bearing, whereas more flexible constructs with low
stiffness are load sharing.

Spectrum of Stability
Relative stability is conferred by a fixation construct that permits controlled fracture
motion and promotes secondary bone healing. Cast immobilization, bracing, external
fixation, intramedullary nailing, and bridge plating provide relative stability to the
fracture site (Figure 1).
Fracture stabilization with interfragmentary compression confers an environment of
absolute stability (with no fracture motion) and promotes primary bone healing (Figure
2).
Constructs with high stiffness and high strength (such as compression and locking
plates) act as load-bearing implants and assume 100% of the functional loads.
Constructs with low stiffness and high strength (such as intramedullary nails and
external fixators) act as load-sharing implants and allow functional loading to be shared
by the fracture site after adequate callus bridging has occurred.2

Working Length
The distance between the most distal fixation in the proximal fracture fragment and the most
proximal fixation in the distal fracture fragment is defined as the fixation construct working
length.

Working Length
Working length of a fracture construct is inversely proportional to fracture stability. The
shorter the working length, the more rigid the construct; the longer the working length,
the more flexible the construct. Working length is most relevant in plating comminuted
metaphyseal fractures (ie, distal femur, proximal and distal tibia). Management of
comminuted metaphyseal fractures typically involves creating an environment for

beneficial because the more flexible construct allows motion that promotes secondary
bone healing (Figure 3). Unfortunately, the exact working length required for secondary
bone healing of comminuted fractures is unknown. If the goal of the construct is to
create an environment for secondary bone healing and if the working length is too short,
then the resulting construct may be too rigid and the fracture may progress to
nonunion. Conversely, if the working length is too long, the resulting construct may be
too flexible and the fracture may progress to nonunion. Often, union or failed union
indicate if the working length was appropriate for the specific fracture2 (Resource 3).
Figure 3 Preoperative (A), 8-week postoperative (B), and 6-month postoperative (C) AP
radiographs of a comminuted metaphyseal fracture of the distal femur managed via
bridge plating. The working length is defined as the distance between the distalmost
screw in the proximal fracture fragment and the proximalmost screw in the distal
fracture fragment. The long working length depicted allows for increased construct
flexibility and promotes secondary bone healing with callus. The unicortical plate was
placed to maintain reduction before definitive plate placement. This is performed with as
little soft-tissue dissection as possible because bridge plating comminuted fractures
should preserve the soft-tissue envelope around the fracture site. (Courtesy of Scott P.
Ryan, MD, Boston, MA.)

Biomechanics of Fixation Constructs
Biomechanics of Plate and Screw Fixation
Modern plate and screw fixation includes nonlocked and locked constructs.

Biomechanics of Plate and Screw Fixation
Nonlocking plate fixation is a construct that relies on friction between the bone and the
plate to provide stability and an environment for healing. As nonlocking plates are
loaded, they convert axial loads into shear stress at the plate-bone interface. These loads
are countered by friction between the bone and the plate. As a nonlocking screw is
tightened down, the torque applied generates an axial force along the screw, fixing the
plate to the bone. This axial force is known as the force normal to the plate. Frictional
force is equal to the product of the frictional coefficient between plate and bone and the
force normal to the plate. Nonlocking construct stability depends on the frictional force
between the plate and bone. If the load at the fracture site exceeds the frictional force
between the plate and bone, then the load is shifted to the screw-plate interface and
may result in construct failure in the form of screw toggling or pullout.
Locking fixation constructs are fixed-angle devices providing angular stability. They do
not rely on friction forces between the bone and plate; rather, loads are transferred
directly from the screws to the plate. Osteoporotic bone or comminuted bone cannot
tolerate sufficient screw torque to generate enough normal force to prevent plate and
fracture motion via friction. In these scenarios, locking fixation constructs are beneficial.
Locking plates improve fracture fixation in patients in whom fracture pattern,
comminution, or bone quality do not permit sufficient screw purchase to allow for the
bone-plate friction necessary for nonlocking constructs to be successful. Locking plates
convert shear stress to compressive stress at the screw-bone interface. In contrast to
nonlocked constructs, fixed-angle locked constructs lead to more uniform distribution of
stresses at all screw-bone interfaces. The strength of fixation is the combination of all
screw-bone interfaces in a locking construct. This differs from nonlocking constructs, in
which the strength of fixation may depend on the axial stiffness or pullout strength of a
single screw.4

Plate stiffness is determined by its material properties and thickness. Stainless steel
plates are twice as stiff as titanium plates. Axial stiffness is proportional to plate
thickness, and bending stiffness is proportional to plate thickness to the third power.
Plate length, screw position, and number of screws may influence the stiffness of a plate
and screw construct. Increasing the distance between screws (screw span) increases
bending stiffness. Torsional stiffness is increased by increasing the number of screws
(screw density) but not screw position.5 Longer plates with fewer screws demonstrate
increased bending stiffness relative to shorter plates with more screws.6 Increasing the
number of cortices of fixation leads to increased overall construct strength because
bicortical screws have increased stability in multiple axes.
Screw bending strength is determined by the inner diameter (root or core diameter).
Screw pullout strength (the ability of a screw to resist pullout) is determined by the
difference between the inner shaft diameter and the outer thread diameter (thread
depth). Pitch refers to the distance between screw threads and determines the distance
a screw advances throughout a 360° turn. Pitch and thread depth also determine the
maximum torque tolerated before thread stripping (Resources 4 and 5).
Biomechanics of Intramedullary Nails
Intramedullary nails are commonly used for long bone fracture fixation; they act as internal
splints with load-sharing properties.

Biomechanics of Intramedullary Nails
Intramedullary nails are used to achieve relative fracture stability and restore length,
alignment, and rotation of long bones, such as the femur and tibia. After fracture
stabilization, intramedullary nails bear most of the load initially, and load bearing is
gradually transferred to bone as fracture healing progresses. Physiologic loads acting on
intramedullary nails include torsion, compression, and tension. The structural stiffness
of an intramedullary nail is determined by its material properties, cross-sectional shape,
diameter, and curvature. Torsional rigidity of an intramedullary nail is determined by its

cross-sectional shape, diameter, degree of contact in the medullary canal, and nail
slotting. Torsional rigidity is proportional to the nail radius to the fourth power. Nail
contact in the medullary canal creates a frictional force to limit movement between the
nail and the bone. Nail slotting leads to reduced torsional rigidity; therefore, slotted nails
are no longer used in current practice. The bending rigidity of an intramedullary nail is
determined by the nail diameter and is proportional to the radius to the third power7
(Resource 6).
Biomechanics of External Fixation
External fixation is commonly used as a temporary stabilization measure in orthopaedic
trauma patients but also may be used for definitive fixation

Biomechanics of External Fixation
External fixation typically is used for acute fractures with considerable soft-tissue
damage. Stable external fixation constructs have low to moderate stiffness, limiting
shear and torque forces but allowing a high degree of micromotion at the fracture site
(relative stability). Therefore, they can maintain fracture reduction and length as the soft-
tissue envelope heals.8
The two most commonly external fixation constructs are unilateral (or monolateral)
external fixation and ring-fixator (circular) systems. Unilateral external fixators typically
are used for temporary stabilization with a goal of maintaining length and providing
resistance to bending. If unilateral frames are used for definitive fixation, a greater need
exists for stability of the construct. This can be achieved by using larger-diameter pins,
increasing the pin spread on each side of the fracture (ie, one pin close to the fracture
and a second pin far away), adding pins in different planes, adding more pins on both
sides of the fracture, keeping the construct as close to the bone as possible, and stacking
the rods (Figure 4). The stiffness of circular ring external fixation constructs is
determined by wire diameter, wire number and orientation, ring diameter, and ring
number. Large wire diameter, increased number of wires, wires perpendicular to one

Pin-Site Care
No evidence-based consensus is available on the most effective pin-site care regimen to
reduce infection. Small incisions with minimal gapping around the pin site facilitate healing


Pin-Site Care
Compressive gauze wrap dressings should be applied to the pin site immediately
postoperatively and left in place for 10 to 14 days postoperatively. These dressings limit
motion between the pin and the skin and prevent the accumulation of fluid. If drainage
from the pin sites is noted in the immediate postoperative period, then dressings should
be changed daily. If the pin sites and dressings have remained dry until follow-up, then
then dressings are removed, and pin sites are checked. If the pin sites are healed
without drainage or erythema, no specific care is required, and the patient may shower
with the frame if desired. If erythema without drainage is present, then pin care should
be initiated two to three times per day with half-strength hydrogen peroxide applied to
the pin site and dry dressing. If erythema with serous drainage is present, then pin care
should continue with the addition of an oral antibiotic agent to cover skin flora.
Management is the same if purulent drainage is noted; however, the pin sites should be
followed more closely. If loosening of the pin with purulence is noted and osteolysis is
observed on radiographs, then the pin should be removed, and local wound care should
continue. If a sequestrum observed on radiographs or considerable erythema and
purulent drainage are present, then débridement should be performed, and cultures
obtained to direct specific antibiotic management.
Screw Types and Functions
Cortical Screws
Cortical screws are designed to maximize purchase in dense cortical bone; therefore, they
have a relatively small pitch and short thread depth to enhance stripping torque.
Cancellous Screws
Cancellous screws are designed to maximize purchase in porous metaphyseal bone; therefore,
they have a large pitch and greater thread depth.
Lag Screws

Lag screws produce compression between fracture fragments by gaining purchase in the far
fracture fragment while gliding through the near fracture fragment.

Lag Screws
The two methods of lag screw insertion are lag by technique and lag by design. To
achieve lag by technique, a glide hole larger than or equal to the outer diameter of the
screw is drilled in the near fragment, and a hole equal to the inner diameter of the screw
is drilled in the far fragment. A fully threaded screw can glide through the near fragment
with no thread purchase and engage the far fragment to achieve interfragmentary
compression. To achieve lag by design, a partially threaded cortical or, more commonly,
cancellous screw is used. The threads of the distal portion of the screw engage the far
fragment as the smooth proximal portion glides through the near fragment to achieve
compression (Resource 9).
Positional Screws
Positional screws are used to hold fracture fragments in a neutral position without obtaining
compression.
Locking Screws
Locking screws contain threads on the screw head that engage with threads in a locking plate
hole to create a fixed-angle construct.
Headless Compression Screws
Headless screws use the concept of differing thread pitch to obtain compression (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Image shows the Synthes 3.0-mm headless compression screw, which consists of a


Headless Compression Screws
The thread pitch of the distal aspect of the screw is larger than the thread pitch of the
proximal aspect of the screw. The larger pitch of the distal aspect of the screw allows this
portion to advance farther through the far fracture fragment relative to the proximal
aspect within the near fracture, achieving fracture compression.
Cannulated Screws
Cannulated screws are hollow, which allow them to be placed over a guidewire.
However, to have a hollow core, the inner diameter of a cannulated screw is increased relative
to the outer diameter, thereby decreasing thread depth and pullout strength.
Plate Types and Functions

Neutralization Plates
Neutralization plates are placed after fracture compression via lag screw fixation to neutralize
torsional and bending forces (Resource 10, Figure 2).
Compression Plates
Compression plating of simple transverse or short oblique fracture patterns is performed by
placing an eccentric screw in plate holes, which translates the plate along the surface of the
bone as the screw engages the plate to provide compression.
For compression plating of transverse fractures, the plate must be pre-bent, with the concave
side applied facing the bone. This allows compression forces to be uniformly distributed across
the fracture. Failure to pre-bend the plate will lead to compression directly under the plate
with distraction at the opposite cortex.
Antiglide Plates
Antiglide plating is used for fracture patterns susceptible to shear forces to prevent
shortening.

Antiglide Plates
In traditional antiglide plating, screws are only placed proximal to the fracture with no
distal screws. The apex screw, or the screw closest to the fracture, is the most important
screw because it sets the plate position on the bone and prevents the gliding or sliding
of the fractured fragment during axial loading. Most often, antiglide plates are
undercontoured, and placement of the screws leads to contouring of the plate to the
bone and provides a reduction force to prevent fracture shortening. In contrast to
buttress plating, antiglide plating does not compress at the adjacent joint (Figures 6 and
7).

Buttress Plates
Buttress plating is used to produce compression in vertically oriented partial articular
fractures.

Buttress Plates

Buttress plating is similar in concept to antiglide plating. An undercontoured plate
generates compression as the apex screw (placed just adjacent to the apex of the
fracture) is tightened down. However, in buttress plating, additional lag screws can be
placed across the fractured fragment in addition to screws intended to support a
reconstructed joint surface (ie, tibial plateau fracture; Figure 8).
Figure 8 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) AP radiographs of a tibial plateau
fracture managed with the use of a buttress plate. The buttress plate is able to generate
compression at the fracture site and accommodates additional screws intended to
support the joint surface. (Courtesy of Scott P. Ryan, MD, Boston, MA.)
Tension Band Plates
Tension band constructs convert tensile forces into compressive forces; therefore, they may
be used to manage transverse fractures that fail in tension.


Tension Band Plates
Certain periarticular fractures, such as the olecranon and patellar fractures, are
amenable to tension band fixation. At these sites, the convex side of the bone is subject
to tension, whereas the concave side is subject to compression. Tension band constructs
convert tensile forces at the convex side into compressive forces on the concave side.
Tension band fixation can be achieved via plate or, commonly, wire fixation. These
constructs prevent fracture distraction on the tension side and, therefore, create
compression across the fracture site.
Bridge Plates
Bridge plating is used for the management of comminuted metaphyseal or diaphyseal
fractures

Bridge Plates
Rather than achieve anatomic reduction and compression (as with other plate and screw
constructs), bridge plates simply bridge or bypass an area of comminution. Therefore,
comminuted fractures managed via bridge plate fixation heal in an environment of
relative stability via secondary bone healing (Figure 3). Bridge plating does not require
locking plate fixation and can be performed with nonlocking plate constructs.
Locking Plates
Locking plates are a type of plate and do not imply function. The manner in which the plate is
applied determines plate function. Locking plates have threaded screw holes that match the
threads on the locking screw heads and allow the screws to lock to the plate, thereby creating
a fixed-angle construct. Fixed-angle constructs are associated with several advantages for
certain types of fractures

9/3/26, 7:30 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000058


Locking Plates
The indications for the use of fixed-angle constructs with locking plates and screws
include short-segment periarticular fractures (ie, distal femur or proximal tibia fractures)
in which multiple fixed-angle screws are required for fixation in the short segment;
fixation in osteoporotic bone; or use of the plate as an internal external fixator, in which
the plate is off the bone and the mode of stability is the fixed angle rather than friction
between the plate and the bone, which is done during standard plating (ie, nonlocked).
This particular construct can be used in distal femur or proximal tibia fractures if the
contour of the plate does not match the bone.9 For distal femur or proximal tibia
fractures with metaphyseal comminution, fixed-angle constructs (such as locking plates)
are critical in plating unilaterally because nonlocking plates are prone to high rates of
varus collapse. Locking plates can be used in various manners, and the term locking
plate does not necessarily infer function in the classic sense (ie, neutralization, antiglide,
bridge, buttress). Note that locking screw density (or the number of locking screws
divided by the number of holes in the plate) should be less than 0.5 to prevent construct
that is overly stiff.
A hybrid construct refers to constructs that use locking and nonlocking screws. These
can be used in two different scenarios: during the plating of metaphyseal fractures,
locking screws are placed in the short, metaphyseal segment, and nonlocking screws can
be placed in the diaphysis if the plate is planned to be on the bone; or if locking screws
are used to protect nonlocking screws during compression plating. In this construct,
nonlocking screws are used first to achieve fracture compression and secure the plate to
the bone. Locking screws are then placed on both sides of the fracture, which increases
the resistance of the nonlocking screws to failure. The addition of locking screws can
protect adjacent nonlocking screws from loosening during cyclical loading. This
technique is advantageous in osteoporotic bone, in which adequate fixation may not be
possible with the use of nonlocking screws alone (Resources 11 and 12).

Intramedullary nails may be used to stabilize fractures in the diaphyseal and metaphyseal
regions of long bones (Resource 13).

Intramedullary Nailing of Metaphyseal Versus Diaphyseal Fractures
Transverse diaphyseal long bone fractures rely on fixation stability based on nail cortical
contact at the isthmus. In diaphyseal fractures, nails with adequate cortical contact at
the isthmus will result in fracture reduction as the nail is passed. Oblique and
comminuted fracture patterns and metaphyseal fractures depend on interlocking screws
for stability. In metaphyseal fractures, reduction must be attained before reaming and
nail passage to prevent eccentric reaming and allow the nail to be advanced centrally
into the distal fracture fragment.10 Failure to do this or to obtain the proper starting
point will result in malreduction as the nail passes into the isthmus. Blocking screws can
be used to prevent malreduction of metaphyseal fractures during nailing because they
decrease the width of the metaphyseal medullary canal, facilitate reduction, limit bone
translation relative to the nail, and increase the overall stability of the construct.11
Blocking screws may be oriented in the sagittal and/or coronal plane and should be
placed on the concave side of the deformity.
Intramedullary Nail Starting Points
Antegrade femoral nails can be performed via piriformis fossa or trochanteric entry.
Retrograde femoral nails are inserted through the intercondylar notch.
Tibial nailing may be performed via four different approaches; however, the starting point is
the same regardless.

Intramedullary Nail Starting Points
The piriformis fossa is directly in line with the femoral canal and is used as the starting
point for straight antegrade nails. The ideal starting point for insertion of a piriformis
entry antegrade femoral nail is the medial border of the greater trochanter in the

Alternatively, trochanteric entry nails are commonly used. These nails are designed with
a small lateral proximal bend of 4° to 6° to facilitate insertion through the tip of the
greater trochanter (Figure 10). The advantage of trochanteric entry nails is easier access
to the starting point, especially in patients with obesity. For subtrochanteric proximal
femur fractures, the starting point must be just medial to the tip of the greater
trochanter because a lateral entry point will lead to varus malreduction12 (Figure 11).

The starting point for a retrograde femoral nail is determined radiographically. On the
lateral view, it should be directly in line with the medullary canal at the apex of the
Blumensaat line. This correlates to a position 6 to 12 mm anterior to the femoral
insertion of the posterior cruciate ligament. On the AP view, the starting point is slightly
medial to the intercondylar sulcus, in line with the medullary canal. The angle typically is
5° to 9° of valgus relative to the joint line (Figure 12).

The standard approach for tibial nailing involves nailing in flexion via an infrapatellar
approach medial, lateral, or through the patellar tendon. Three other techniques have
been developed for nailing of proximal and distal fractures that allow the procedure to
be performed from full extension to 30° of flexion. These techniques include original,
semi-extended nailing in 15° to 30° of flexion with a partial medial parapatellar
arthrotomy; suprapatellar nailing, which involves an approach above the patella through
the quadriceps and knee joint; and lateral parapatellar nailing in 15° to 30° of flexion.
More recent evidence has shown improved alignment with suprapatellar semi-extended
nailing of distal tibia fractures. Additional proposed advantages of suprapatellar or semi-
extended nailing include ease of obtaining the starting point and intraoperative AP
radiographs and maintained fracture reduction. The starting point does not differ based

Intramedullary Reaming
Intramedullary reaming increases the contact area between a nail and cortical bone and allows
for the insertion of a larger-diameter nail.

Intramedullary Reaming

Intramedullary reaming serves to increase the contact area between an intramedullary
nail and cortical bone. One mm of reaming increases the cortical contact area by 38%.7
Reaming also allows for the insertion of a larger-diameter nail, affording increased
torsional and bending rigidity. Therefore, reaming leads to increased biomechanical
fixation stability compared with unreamed nails. In a multicenter, prospective
randomized trial of 224 patients who underwent reamed or unreamed intramedullary
nailing of an open or closed femoral shaft fracture, a 4.5 times greater relative risk of
nonunion was associated with unreamed nails.13 In a multicenter, blind randomized trial
of 1,226 patients with a tibial shaft fracture, reamed intramedullary nailing for the
management of closed fractures led to fewer revision surgery procedures at a follow-up
of 1 year than unreamed nailing14 (Resources 16 and 17).
Interlocking Screw Fixation
Static interlocking screws function to maintain length, alignment, and rotation after
intramedullary nailing.

Interlocking Screw Fixation
The number of interlocking screws necessary for intramedullary nailing is determined by
fracture location, comminution, and fit of the nail within the medullary canal. Placing
interlocking screws farther from the fracture site increases rotational stability.
Interlocking screws are subject to four-point bending loads and, therefore, should have
the largest diameter possible. Biomechanical studies indicate that femoral
intramedullary nail constructs with only one distal locking screw have considerably lower
fatigue strength than two-screw constructs. The orientation of proximal interlocking
screws is particularly important in patients with proximal tibia fractures, with obliquely
oriented screws providing increased stability. Most studies agree that static locking is the
current standard of care for the management of diaphyseal fractures.7 Patients may
safely bear weight on statically locked intramedullary nails in the femur or tibia without
compromising reduction or fixation.15,16
